questions.text: Why does the lesson’s HTTP server compare mirrored method and name headers with the JSON-RPC body before executing a request?

options.A: To let routing headers override any conflicting body fields.
options.B: To ensure routing or policy checks and execution refer to the same operation.
options.C: To authenticate the client using its chosen tool name.
options.D: To recover missing arguments from an earlier connection.

questions.explanation: Header-body equality prevents a gateway from checking one operation while the server executes another.

questions.text: A draft created on replica 1 must remain available when the next request reaches replica 2. Which design fits the lesson’s stateless transport model?

options.A: Keep the draft only in replica 1 and depend on sticky routing.
options.B: Use the next JSON-RPC request ID as the draft’s persistent identity.
options.C: Store the draft only in the current HTTP response stream.
options.D: Return an explicit draft handle backed by shared storage and authorize each use.

questions.explanation: Durable application state needs explicit identity and shared persistence so any replica can load it; each use must still be authorized.

questions.text: In do_POST, the body’s version is unsupported and differs from MCP-Protocol-Version. Other structure and headers are valid. Which check fails first?

options.C: dispatch returns -32601 because the method is never inspected.
options.D: The server accepts the header version and overwrites the body version.

questions.explanation: do_POST validates structure, compares headers, then checks whether the matched version is supported. A version mismatch therefore raises -32020 first.
